judgments.reasoning_cat1: It combines an absolute class-arbitration bar with a 'notwithstanding any other provision herein to the contrary' carve-out reserving validity of that bar to a court, and then a blow-up fallback to court litigation — three moving parts whose interaction is genuinely arguable.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It contradicts Paragraph 1(a), which commits 'the validity and scope of this Arbitration Provision' to arbitration, and its court fallback must be squared with Paragraph 8's void-the-whole-provision rule.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'any other arbitrator ... reasonably satisfactory to us' and the 20-day default giving the drafter the choice are open-ended and one-sidedly drafted, and the paragraph is a sprawling mix of selection rules, fee rules and unrelated usury boilerplate.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Its cap — advancing filing/administrative/hearing fees only 'up to $1000' — sits directly against Paragraph 5, which says that at the customer's request 'we will advance your portion of the arbitration expenses' without any cap.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: It says each party bears its own fees 'but without limitation of any party's ability to recover costs and attorneys' fees to the extent authorized by law', and instructs the arbitrator to entertain Rule 12/56-style motions while applying no rules of civil procedure — internally awkward.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The uncapped advance of Arbitration Fees conflicts with Paragraph 4's $1000 ceiling, and the loser-reimburses rule sits against Paragraph 4's promise that the arbitrator decides who ultimately pays.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'disputes within the scope of such tribunal's jurisdiction' and 'cannot be adjudicated within the jurisdiction of a small claims tribunal' leave the dividing line to be worked out, especially for claims that could have been but were not filed there.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It is the express exception to Paragraph 3 and to 2(b), but its last sentence sending small-claims appeals to arbitration cuts against Paragraph 4's rule that a judgment entered in a lawsuit ends the right to demand arbitration.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A short, definite choice-of-law rule with a clearly stated fallback; nothing ambiguous in the words.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It is consistent with the GOVERNING LAW clause and with the Interstate Commerce stipulation; the Texas fallback is a subordinate condition, not a contradiction.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The blow-up proviso — the whole Arbitration Provision is void if the class-arbitration bar is 'deemed invalid or unenforceable' — turns on who deems it and when, and cuts against the severability sentence immediately preceding it.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It conflicts with the ENTIRE AGREEMENT clause, which says an invalid provision 'shall be reformed if practicable' and 'shall not in any way affect the remaining provisions', and it overlaps imperfectly with Paragraph 3's own court fallback.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The text as executed is partly illegible and the opt-out window (ninety calendar days) with its content requirements is the sort of mechanism whose compliance is routinely fought over.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It is the mechanism the jury-waiver clause alludes to as a right to 'reject' the arbitration agreement, and a customer who opts out is still left bound by the separate WAIVER OF RIGHT TO TRIAL BY JURY clause.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A one-sentence choice of law with a single stated exception; the wording is definite.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Paragraph 7 adds a Texas-arbitration-law fallback that this clause's flat 'governed by the FAA' does not mention — a minor gap rather than a contradiction.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A statutorily framed all-caps warning creating no rights or obligations, so there is nothing to construe.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It is consistent with the short-term installment structure disclosed in the cost terms; no operative provision contradicts it.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Pure regulator contact information; not an operative term.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Nothing elsewhere in the instrument bears on it, although the pre-suit notice clause conditions claims generally.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'the entire agreement between you and us relating to the subject matter' and the reform-if-practicable severability are boilerplate, but 'reformed if practicable' is an indefinite standard.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Its severability rule conflicts with Arbitration Paragraph 8, which voids the whole Arbitration Provision if the class waiver falls, and its integration language sits against the separate disclosure statement and Notices of Cancellation the signature block acknowledges.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The acknowledgment list is so corrupted in the executed text that clause (a) cannot be read at all, and the warranties ('no intention to file a petition', account is 'legitimate, open, and active') are subjective and open-ended.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It recites receipt of a separate disclosure statement and two Notices of Cancellation, which the ENTIRE AGREEMENT clause's integration language does not mention, and it certifies assent to an Arbitration Provision the opt-out clause allows the customer to reject.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'BEFORE MIDNIGHT OF THE THIRD DAY AFTER THE DATE OF THE TRANSACTION' fixes a deadline but 'the date of the transaction' is not defined anywhere in the instrument.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The attached Notice of Cancellation measures the same period 'within three days after the date the contract is signed' and then names a fixed date, so the three formulations must be reconciled.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A short grant of a three-day cancellation right; the only softness is 'within three days after the date the contract is signed'.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It uses a different reference point from the NOTICE clause ('date of the transaction'), and the LOC clause conditions automatic revocation on the customer 'timely' exercising this right.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A single definite obligation to return payments within ten days; the only mechanical flaw is the missing space in 'within10 days'.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It assumes payments made to the seller, whereas the cost terms show the CAB fee is financed by and paid through the Lender, leaving unclear what would be returned on cancellation.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: It states a method and a fixed calendar deadline; 'or other written notice' is a small open end but the instruction is otherwise definite.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The 04/12/2012 deadline squares with the 4/9/2012 execution date and the three-day rule in the NOTICE clause, so the pieces cohere.
